newsitem.title: UK: UK Audit Bureau may expand newspaper figures.
newsitem.headline: UK Audit Bureau may expand newspaper figures.

text.p: Britain's Audit Bureau of Circulation (ABC) said it may expand the way it reports newspaper circulation figures to reflect a growth in subscription sales and to settle a simmering dispute in Britain's newspaper circulation wars.

"Subscriptions are no longer deemed to be an immaterial element of the circulation," Anthony Peacham, spokesman for the ABC, told Reuters in a phone interview. "There are suggestions that subscription sales be separated out."

The ABC currently reports the total circulation of Britain's national newspapers and also breaks out the total number of copies sold at the full cover price, the total number sold at a lesser rate, and bulk sales.
Subscription sales, even when the rate represents a discount from a newspaper's cover price, are included in copies sold at the full cover price.
Peacham said the ABC's executive committee will probably meet again fairly shortly to discuss whether subscription sales should be separated out from copies sold at the full cover price.

Subscription sales have become a hot topic since the Telegraph Group, part of Hollinger Inc and publisher of the Daily Telegraph and Sunday Telegraph, in late 1996 began to aggressively market subscriptions. The offer, made only to specially targeted readers, undercuts the price of buying the paper by single copy. The Telegraph currently has about 100,000 subscribers.

The Telegraph's strategy is a sharp divide from Britain's other broadsheet national newspapers, which have lured readers with various special promotions since Rupert Murdoch, whose News Corp Ltd publishes the Times and Sunday Times, ended a fierce price war in 1995. The Times has continued to sell its Monday paper for 10 pence, compared to 35p for the Thursday through Friday editions.
The Times has complained repeatedly to the ABC about inclusion of the Telegraph's discounted subscription sales in full-price circulation figures.

The row had become so heated that the ABC chose to omit any figures for the Telegraph when it initially issued its November report. The ABC later decided to included the subscription sales in Telegraph's full figures, but the Times has continued to protest.
The Telegraph began its subscription drive in the 1996 third quarter, aimed at turning occasional readers of the newspaper into regular readers.

"We made the ... offer to people who were profiled as likely to want to read us but not regular readers," Hugo Drayton marketing director of the Telegraph Group, told Reuters. "People who were buying it one or two times a week or who have a (certain) lifestyle profile ... ABC1 adults, female and male professionals. They're the people our advertisers want to reach."
Drayton said the subscription offer builds reader loyalty in a way that both reduced cover prices and special promotions do not.
"What it shows to advertisers is we're not interested in quick bangs that sort of fall off again," he said. "Our advertisers know they're not wasting money on people they're not targeting."

Drayton, however, said no direct correlation could be drawn between advertising and circulation activity. "To draw a direct line that new subscriptins are bringing in new subscribers I couldn't say," he said.
